# Laravel change database connection at run time

In many applications, a single `config/database.php` file defines multiple connections, yet the default behavior ties your application to one specific driver per environment. Switching from, say, `mysql` to `pgsql` or toggling between read replicas and master nodes usually requires reloading the server or clearing caches. However, there are legitimate scenarios where you need to alter the active database connection dynamically within a running process without restarting the web server.

Laravel handles this through its Service Container and the underlying PDO abstraction, but the mechanism depends entirely on how you invoke it. If you attempt to simply reassign the global `DB` facade variable, you will encounter immediate issues because the underlying PDO instance is already bound and cached in memory. The framework initializes a connection object at the moment you first call `DB::connection()`, and subsequent calls without arguments retrieve that same instance rather than creating a fresh one for a different configuration.

To change the active connection at runtime, you must explicitly tell the container to instantiate a new connection using a specific name defined in your configuration. This is achieved by passing a string argument to the `DB::connection()` method. For example, if you have configured a secondary named connection like `secondary` in your `database.php` file, you can switch contexts like this:

```php
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

// Switches to the 'secondary' connection defined in config/database.php
$connection = DB::connection('secondary');

// Now all subsequent operations on $connection use that specific driver and host
$connection->table('users')->get();
```

This approach does not affect other parts of your application. The global `DB` facade continues to point to the default connection unless you explicitly switch it again. This is crucial for maintaining consistency across a monolithic codebase where different services might need to talk to different repositories simultaneously.

The most common pitfall occurs when developers expect the global `DB` facade to automatically update their state after calling `DB::connection('new_name')`. They often write code assuming that once a switch happens, all future queries in the same scope will use the new connection. In reality, unless you reassign the facade or pass the specific connection instance to your repository classes, the old PDO object remains active for any global calls.

If you are working with Eloquent models, switching connections becomes even more nuanced. Models typically bind their own database connections during instantiation. Simply changing the global `DB` connection won't retroactively update an existing model instance unless you explicitly change its configuration. You can do this by calling `app('db')` or using the facade's switch method if available in your version, but a cleaner pattern is to create new Eloquent instances that are aware of the intended connection from the start:

```php
$user = DB::connection('secondary')->table('users')->first();
```

Alternatively, you can adjust the model's connection property directly, though this requires careful handling to avoid unintended side effects in a multi-tenant or read-replica setup.

When deciding whether to implement dynamic switching, consider the performance implications. While Laravel caches connection information, every time you instantiate a new PDO object via `DB::connection('name')`, the framework initializes the connection driver, which involves opening a socket and running authentication checks against your database server. This latency is negligible for occasional use but can accumulate if your application performs thousands of rapid context switches in a tight loop.

For high-frequency operations, it is often better to resolve the appropriate repository or service instance at the beginning of a request or job rather than switching connections mid-operation. Always verify that your `database.php` configuration includes the new connection name and that the corresponding credentials are valid for the target environment.

If you need further guidance on managing complex database configurations in Laravel, check out https://laravelcompany.com for additional resources on optimizing your data layer architecture.
